description: Side-by-side reviews of smart home gear, sorted by the radio it talks on. Start with the protocol that fits your house, then pick the switches, sensors, and locks that run on it.

protocols.name: Z-Wave
protocols.summary: Low-power mesh on a sub-GHz band, built for home automation and nothing else.
protocols.verdict: The safest pick for a hub-based setup that has to keep working for years. Every certified device talks to every certified controller, and its band stays out of Wi-Fi's way.
pros: Sub-GHz radio doesn't compete with Wi-Fi or Zigbee on 2.4 GHz
Lower frequency gets through walls and floors better than 2.4 GHz
Mandatory certification, so devices from different brands work together
Every mains-powered device repeats the signal and extends the mesh
S2 security is required on newer certified devices
Z-Wave Long Range reaches outbuildings and supports up to 4,000 devices
cons: Needs a hub or USB controller; there's no phone-only setup
Devices usually cost more than Zigbee or Wi-Fi equivalents
Frequencies are regional, so a US device won't work on an EU controller
Low bandwidth rules out cameras and anything streaming
Classic mesh tops out at 232 devices and 4 hops

protocols.name: Zigbee
protocols.summary: Cheap, low-power 2.4 GHz mesh with the widest catalog of small sensors.
protocols.verdict: The budget king for sensors and bulbs. Pair it with a good coordinator and plenty of plug-in repeaters and it's rock solid.

facts.power: Very low, coin-cell sensors last 1-2 years
facts.best_for: Lots of cheap sensors, bulbs, buttons

pros: Sensors and buttons are among the cheapest on the market
Huge catalog from Aqara, IKEA, Philips Hue, Sonoff, Third Reality, and others
Mains-powered devices act as routers and strengthen the mesh
Coin-cell battery devices run for a year or more
Works fully local with Home Assistant (ZHA or Zigbee2MQTT)
cons: Shares the 2.4 GHz band with Wi-Fi, so channel planning matters
Some brands bend the spec; Aqara devices can drop off third-party routers
Needs a coordinator (hub or USB stick)
Brand hubs like Hue only accept their own approved devices
Bulbs used as repeaters break the mesh when someone flips the wall switch

protocols.name: Wi-Fi
protocols.summary: Uses the router you already own. No hub, lots of bandwidth, lots of power draw.
protocols.verdict: Right for cameras, doorbells, and anything plugged in. Wrong for battery sensors, and a few dozen devices can overload a cheap router.
pros: No hub; it joins the network you already have
Enough bandwidth for live video and audio
Widest choice of brands and the lowest entry prices
Setup is usually an app and a few taps
cons: Power hungry; battery Wi-Fi sensors need frequent charging
Many devices only support 2.4 GHz, which complicates setup on mixed-band routers
Dozens of devices can overload consumer routers
Many products depend on the maker's cloud and stop working if it shuts down
No mesh between devices; range is whatever your router covers

protocols.name: Bluetooth
protocols.summary: Phone-to-device and short range. Easy to set up, hard to reach from outside the room.
protocols.verdict: Fine for one-room gadgets you control from your phone. For whole-house automation, plan on a hub or Bluetooth proxies.

facts.topology: Point-to-point (Bluetooth Mesh exists but is rare)
facts.hub: No for phone control; yes for remote access
facts.best_for: Locks, trackers, sensors near a hub

pros: Pairs straight to your phone with no hub or network
Bluetooth LE sips power, so sensors run for months or years
Keeps working when the internet is down
Home Assistant can extend coverage with cheap ESP32 Bluetooth proxies
cons: Short range, often a single room through walls
No remote control unless a hub, bridge, or proxy is in range
Bluetooth Mesh has little product support for home automation
Many devices work only through the maker's own app

protocols.name: Thread
protocols.summary: IP-based, self-healing 2.4 GHz mesh. The low-power radio behind most new Matter devices.
protocols.verdict: The best bet for new battery devices if you already own a border router. The catalog is still smaller than Zigbee's or Z-Wave's.
pros: Every device gets an IPv6 address, so there's no proprietary translation layer
Self-healing mesh with no single point of failure if you run more than one border router
Low power with fast response times
Border routers are built into devices many people already own: HomePod mini, Apple TV 4K, Nest Hub (2nd gen), and some Echo models
cons: Needs a Thread border router
Border routers from different ecosystems don't always share one network
Smaller product catalog than Zigbee or Z-Wave
Shares the 2.4 GHz band with Wi-Fi and Zigbee
Newer standard, so firmware and pairing bugs still show up

protocols.name: Matter
protocols.summary: A shared language, not a radio. Runs over Wi-Fi, Thread, or Ethernet and works across Apple, Google, Amazon, SmartThings, and Home Assistant.
protocols.verdict: Buy Matter devices when you can, because they keep your options open. Check that the features you need are in the spec before you buy.

facts.hub: A Matter controller (most smart speakers and hubs qualify)
facts.best_for: Anyone mixing ecosystems or avoiding lock-in

pros: One device works with Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa, SmartThings, and Home Assistant
Multi-admin lets several ecosystems control the same device at once
Local control by design, no cloud needed for day-to-day use
Setup is a QR code scan in whichever app you prefer
cons: Only device types in the current spec are supported, so advanced features often stay in the maker's app
Each platform exposes a different slice of what a device can do
Pairing and multi-admin bugs are still common
Matter over Thread devices still need a Thread border router

protocols.name: Lutron Clear Connect
protocols.summary: Lutron's own RF used by Caseta and RadioRA. Proprietary and very reliable.
protocols.verdict: If you only care about lighting and want it to just work, this is the benchmark. Expect to stay inside the Lutron catalog.

facts.topology: Star to a Lutron bridge or processor
facts.hub: Yes, a Lutron Smart Bridge or processor
facts.power: Pico remotes run about 10 years on a coin cell

pros: Very reliable; its band has almost no competing traffic
Dimmers work with a wide range of LED bulbs without flicker
Pico remotes run for years and need no wiring
Integrates with HomeKit, Alexa, Google, SmartThings, and Home Assistant through the bridge
cons: Only Lutron devices join the network
Requires a Lutron bridge or processor
Lighting and shades only; no general-purpose sensors
Costs more per switch than most Zigbee or Wi-Fi options

protocols.name: 433 MHz RF
protocols.summary: Simple one-way radio found in cheap sensors, weather stations, and remotes.
protocols.verdict: Great for cheap outdoor sensors you only need to read. Skip it for anything security-related.

facts.hub: Yes, an RF bridge or SDR receiver

pros: Very cheap sensors
Long range through walls and out to the yard
Batteries last a long time
A $30 SDR dongle running rtl_433 can read hundreds of device models
cons: No common standard; each brand uses its own encoding
Mostly one-way, with no confirmation that a command arrived
Typically no encryption, so signals can be sniffed or replayed
Needs an RF bridge or SDR to get into a smart home system
